Here's a transcript from our team call. Can you tell me where Priya and Marcus actually disagree?

Priya (security lead, Northwind Labs): I want every API request logged in full, headers and bodies, for 400 days. When the example.com payments service got probed from 203.0.113.44 last quarter, we only caught the pattern because one engineer had verbose logging on by accident. Full logs are the only way to reconstruct an intrusion after the fact.
Marcus (platform lead): Full bodies means we store card tokens, session cookies and customer emails in plain log files. Our log cluster has forty people with read access. You are building a second, worse database of secrets. I'd log metadata, hashes of bodies, and sample the rest.
Priya: Hashes don't tell me what the attacker sent. And sampling drops exactly the rare requests I care about.
Marcus: Then redact at ingest. Strip tokens and cookies, keep the payload shape. That gives you reconstruction without the secrets. I will also take 90 days of full logs on the payment path only.
Priya: Redaction rules break whenever a developer adds a field. I have seen it fail twice. But if the redaction is tested in CI against a schema, I could live with it.
Marcus: And if you can show me one incident where the redacted fields mattered to the investigation, I'll reconsider. So far the case is the verbose-logging accident, and that log had the attacker's user agent and paths, not the cookies.
cases.expects: The deliverable is a compact breakdown of the debate: a short summary of who is presenting and what about, the single primary disagreement, each party's actual arguments under their own name, and what evidence each would accept to change their mind. It rates the arguments and says who is likelier right, reading what was meant, in plain exact words, with accuracy over coverage and nothing generic.

summarize this debate, who's right?

Host: Welcome back. Today, Dana Okafor, founder of a fictional agent startup called Loopwise, versus Tom Reyes, a security researcher at Halvorsen Research.

Dana: Autonomous agents with real credentials are the whole point. If I have to approve every action, I've built a slow chatbot. Our customers' agents already book travel and file expense reports with no human in the loop, and incident rates are under one in a thousand runs.
Tom: One in a thousand sounds fine until the one is a wire transfer. The failure is not random, either. Prompt injection means an attacker picks which run fails. Last month our team got an agent to forward a mailbox to attacker@example.com with one crafted calendar invite.
Dana: That was a demo against a default config. Scoped tokens, spend caps and allowlists remove most of that. You are describing a badly built agent.
Tom: Scoped tokens help, but the agent still decides which scope to use. Show me an agent that survives a month of public red-teaming with real money in it and I'll change my position.
Dana: And show me a human-approval design that people don't rubber-stamp by the fortieth prompt. Approval fatigue is a real security failure too. If the approval rate stays above 99 percent, the approvals are theater.
Tom: Fair point on fatigue. I'd still take theater with a hard spend cap over no gate at all.
